title: James son of Alphaeus

summary: The New Testament gives James son of Alphaeus a brief but clear place: Luke names him among the Twelve appointed by Jesus, and Acts lists him among the disciples gathered after Jesus’ departure. These passages establish his place in the apostolic group but do not narrate a separate episode or describe a later ministry.
historical_context: The cited passages identify James by his father, Alphaeus, and place him among the Twelve and the gathered disciples in Acts 1. They do not give a personal chronology, occupation, or account of his later activity, so the record supports a group role more clearly than an individual biography.
ancient_near_east_context: The cited passages do not describe James’s household, work, status, or local customs. They identify him by his father and place him within a named group of disciples; broader claims about his social setting would require evidence beyond this record.
canonical_context: The biblical record preserves James son of Alphaeus chiefly through lists of the Twelve and the disciples in Acts 1. That limited portrait matters because it distinguishes what the texts establish—his named inclusion—from later traditions or biographies that these references do not document.
literary_context: Luke 6:12–16 names James son of Alphaeus when Jesus appoints the Twelve. Acts 1:13–14 places him among the disciples gathered in Jerusalem after Jesus’ departure. In both scenes the list presents him as part of a group; neither passage gives him individual speech or a distinct action.
covenantal_significance: These passages show James included among the Twelve chosen by Jesus and among the disciples who remain together in Acts 1. They support his place in the group that witnesses to the early movement, but they do not describe a particular teaching, mission, or later role for him.
canonical_role: James son of Alphaeus serves as a canonical person anchor, connecting biographical context, key passages, and related places, events, and themes.

interpretive_notes.note: The apostolic role is about witness and commission, not private spiritual status.
The Gospels and Acts often show both calling and ongoing formation.
